### 5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate LiteResearcher-4B on a suite of complex reasoning and agentic search benchmarks,
including GAIA (Mialon et al., [2023](#bib.bib21)), BrowseComp (Wei et al., [2025a](#bib.bib38)), HLE (Phan et al., [2025](#bib.bib27)),
Frames (Krishna et al., [2025](#bib.bib13)), WebWalker (Wu et al., [2025b](#bib.bib41)), Seal-0 (Pham et al., [2026](#bib.bib26)),
and Xbench-DeepSearch-2505 (Chen et al., [2025](#bib.bib4)). For BrowseComp, we randomly sampled 400 examples for evaluation. Evaluation is conducted with online APIs (Serper for search and Jina for browsing), following the same tool setup as prior work (Team et al., [2025c](#bib.bib35)). We compare against leading closed-source foundation models, representative open-source deep-research agents, and AgentCPM-Explore (Chen et al., [2026](#bib.bib2)) as a concurrent lightweight baseline.

All experiments are initialized from Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 (Yang et al., [2025](#bib.bib42)). We first perform a cold-start SFT stage to teach the model basic tool-use capabilities such as query formulation, search invocation, and page browsing (details in Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B SFT Details ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ Contribution of RL over SFT. ‣ Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training. ‣ On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training. ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent")). The RL stage generates rollouts entirely within our local environment, with a global batch size of 128 (on-policy update), generating 8 rollouts per query. The learning rate is fixed at $1\times 10^{-6}$. The maximum response length is initialized at 32K tokens in the first stage and expanded by 16K tokens in each subsequent stage. Our loss function uses neither a KL divergence penalty nor an entropy regularization term.

Table 2: Main results. Comparison across commercial models and open-source deep research agents on eight benchmarks. Best open-source results are in bold. Results without * are evaluated with a 128k context window; results with * use a 64k context window with a memory mechanism that, upon reaching the context limit, calls a summarization model to compress each previous tool interaction step into one sentence.

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent") summarizes the performance of LiteResearcher (4B) across eight benchmarks spanning general-purpose agentic search, multi-hop reasoning, and cross-lingual deep research. From the results, we make the following key observations.

A 4B model trained locally approaches commercial-level performance. LiteResearcher achieves 71.3% on GAIA-Text, matching Claude-4.5-Sonnet (71.2%) and surpassing Tongyi DeepResearch 30B (70.9%) and other open-source models with 8–32B parameters. On Frames, it scores 83.1%, outperforming Claude-4-Sonnet (80.7%) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (80.2%). On Xbench-DS, a comprehensive bilingual benchmark, LiteResearcher reaches 78.0%, the highest among all open-source models and surpassing OpenAI-GPT-5-high (77.8%). These results suggest that the data–environment bottleneck is at least as important as model scale for strong agentic search performance.

Local training matches or exceeds online training. AgentCPM-Explore-4B (Chen et al., [2026](#bib.bib2)), a concurrent 4B model trained on the live internet, is outperformed by LiteResearcher on all 8 benchmarks (e.g., GAIA 71.3% vs. 63.9%, Xbench 78.0% vs. 70.0%). AgentCPM-Explore further reports that online environment instability is a major source of reward noise, limiting its RL gains to only +3.8% over the SFT baseline on GAIA. Our deterministic local environment eliminates such noise, sustaining over 700 stable RL steps with monotonic improvements.

Context length and BrowseComp. BrowseComp requires exceptionally deep browsing chains, often exceeding 20 pages per query. For a 4B model, this frequently exhausts the 128K context window, causing performance degradation (20.3%/28.4% without memory, Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ B.3 Training and Baseline Performance ‣ Appendix B SFT Details ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ Contribution of RL over SFT. ‣ Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training. ‣ On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training. ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent")). A memory mechanism that summarizes prior tool interactions at 64K mitigates this, improving results to 27.5%/32.5%. This gap highlights long-context utilization as a key limitation of small-scale agents, and we report both configurations for transparency.

### 5.3 Analysis and Ablations

#### Local Environment vs. Live Internet.

Over the full RL run, our agents issued 45.8M search queries and 27.4M browse requests—totaling 73.2M tool calls. As shown in Table [5.3](#S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent"), fulfilling this volume through commercial search engines and browser proxies would cost $59K–$243K, whereas our fully local pipeline incurs zero marginal cost. Beyond the cost saving, the 10–46$\times$ latency advantage directly translates to higher rollout throughput, making our local ecosystem a prerequisite—not merely an optimization—for scalable on-policy agentic RL.

#### Effect of Our Synthetic Data.

Our synthesis pipeline produces data diverse enough to cover real-world search patterns and support strong generalization (Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent")): combining our synthetic data with multi-hop data achieves 66.8% on GAIA and 71.0% on Xbench. Removing our synthetic data drops performance to 58.7%/66.3%, confirming that it covers diverse search patterns.

| Training Data | GAIA | Xbench |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Multi-hop only | 58.7% | 66.3% |
| Ours + multi-hop | 66.8% | 71.0% |

Table 4: Effect of our synthetic data.

![Refer to caption](2604.17931v2/x3.png)


Figure 3: On-Policy vs. Off-Policy training reward. On-policy training is more stable and continues to improve throughout training.

#### On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training.

We compare a strictly on-policy algorithm, where each rollout batch is consumed in a single update and then discarded, with a more off-policy algorithm, where each rollout batch is split into multiple mini-batches (e.g., 256 samples into 4 mini-batches) and used for several successive updates. As shown in Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent"), the off-policy variant gains reward much earlier but eventually declines, whereas on-policy training continues to improve more steadily throughout training. Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent") shows that on-policy training achieves higher GAIA validation accuracy (68.9%) than off-policy training (66.8%).

These results suggest that long-horizon Agentic RL is particularly sensitive to off-policy updates. We hypothesize that multiple updates on the same rollout batch introduce policy lag, leading to increasing mismatch between the sampled trajectories and the current policy. In long-horizon search tasks, such mismatch can accumulate along the trajectory, harming optimization stability and ultimately limiting the achievable performance ceiling.

#### Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training.

Single-stage RL saturates once the model exhausts tasks at its current difficulty level; deliberate difficulty escalation is the key to continued improvement. Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training. ‣ On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training. ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent") shows the learning curves of our two-stage strategy. In Stage 1, the model reaches a plateau at 64.7% GAIA accuracy. After transitioning to Stage 2 with adjusted data distribution and targeted complexity, training continues to improve, reaching 68.3% (+3.6%). This indicates that the second stage helps sustain learning beyond the saturation point of the first, enabled by our unlimited synthetic data pool.

![Refer to caption](2604.17931v2/x4.png)


Figure 4: Stage 1 vs. Stage 2. GAIA accuracy (EMA smoothed) during RL training. The two-stage curriculum overcomes the Stage 1 plateau.

#### Contribution of RL over SFT.

The SFT stage uses trajectories generated by Tongyi DeepResearch as the teacher model (Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B SFT Details ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ Contribution of RL over SFT. ‣ Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training. ‣ On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training. ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent")). As shown in Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ B.3 Training and Baseline Performance ‣ Appendix B SFT Details ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ Contribution of RL over SFT. ‣ Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training. ‣ On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training. ‣ Local Environment vs. Live Internet. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent"), SFT alone yields 55.6% on GAIA—still 15.3 points below the teacher’s own 70.9%. The RL stage not only closes this gap but surpasses it, reaching 71.3% (+15.7 over SFT), with consistent gains across all eight benchmarks. This indicates that the primary performance driver is the RL training framework rather than teacher distillation.
